blocks.title: Introduction to the Law of Sines
teacherCues: Draw a non‑right triangle and label sides a, b, c opposite angles A, B, C. Ask: What ratio might be constant?
Write the Law of Sines on the board. Emphasize: works for any oblique triangle, not just right triangles.

discoveryHook.scenario: Surveyors used the Law of Sines to measure the height of Mount Everest more than 150 years ago, within 30 feet of the true height.

explanation: The [[kw:Law of Sines]] says: $$\frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{c}{\sin C}.$$
You can also flip it: $$\frac{\sin A}{a} = \frac{\sin B}{b} = \frac{\sin C}{c}.$$
Use it to find missing sides or angles in any triangle.

visuals.title: When to use Law of Sines

rows.0: Two angles + a side (AAS or ASA)

formulaCard.title: Law of Sines
notes: a opposite A, b opposite B, c opposite C.
Pick two ratios that include the unknown.

examples.title: A – Find missing angle
examples.prompt: In triangle ABC, A = 50°, B = 60°. Find C.

examples.title: B – Set up proportion
examples.prompt: Given a = 10, A = 30°, B = 45°. Set up the proportion to find b.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to your partner: Which two ratios do you use? Why can you leave out the third?
steps: Write: a / sin A = b / sin B.

examples.title: C – Find side c
examples.prompt: From B's triangle, now find c if C = 105°.
steps: Use a / sin A = c / sin C.

confusionCorner.title: Labeling Tip
confusionCorner.body: Always label side a opposite angle A, side b opposite B, side c opposite C. Then the law is [[imp:easy to write]].

questions.prompt: The Law of Sines says a / sin A = b / sin B = c / ___.
hints: It's the sine of the third angle.
Same pattern: side over sine of its opposite angle.

questions.prompt: How many angles do you need to know to use Law of Sines for an AAS triangle? (Enter a number)
hints: You know two angles; the third can be found.

questions.prompt: If A = 50° and B = 60°, then C = ___°.

blocks.title: Solving AAS and ASA Triangles
teacherCues: Draw a triangle with known A, B, and side a. Ask: How do we find b? (use proportion).
Example: A=30°, B=45°, a=32 cm. Find b and c together.

discoveryHook.scenario: A leaning pole casts a 22‑foot shadow at an angle of 43°. By measuring two angles and the shadow, you can find the pole’s height without climbing.

explanation: For AAS or ASA: first find the third angle (C = 180° – A – B).
Use the pair you know (e.g., a and A) to find another side: b = a × (sin B / sin A).

formulaCard.title: Side from a known pair
notes: a and A are a known side-angle pair.
Multiply by sin of the angle opposite the side you want.

examples.title: A – Find b and c
examples.prompt: Given A=49°, B=29°, b=28 ft. Find a and c.
steps: a = b × (sin A / sin B) = 28 × (sin49° / sin29°) ≈ 43.59 ft.
c = b × (sin C / sin B) ≈ 56.49 ft.

examples.title: B – Leaning pole
examples.prompt: Pole tilts 8° from vertical, shadow 22 ft, angle of elevation 43°. Find height.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain: What is angle B? (Hint: vertical line + tilt = 98°). Then apply Law of Sines.

examples.title: C – Find b directly
examples.prompt: Given A=30°, B=45°, a=32 cm. Find b without finding C.
steps: b = a × (sin B / sin A) = 32 × (sin45° / sin30°) ≈ 45.25 cm.

confusionCorner.title: ASA vs AAS
confusionCorner.body: The method is the same: find the third angle, then use the known side-angle pair. The law [[imp:doesn't care]] which arrangement you have.

questions.prompt: To find side b when you know a, A, and B, multiply a by (sin B / sin ___ ).
hints: The denominator is sin of the known angle.
The known side a is opposite A.

questions.prompt: If A = 30°, B = 45°, a = 10, what is b approximately? (Enter a number, e.g., 14.14)
hints: b = a × sin B / sin A = 10 × sin45° / sin30°.

questions.prompt: In the leaning pole problem, the angle between the pole and the vertical is 8°, so angle B = 90° + 8° = ___°.

blocks.title: The Ambiguous Case (SSA)
teacherCues: Draw acute angle A, side b, and a short side a. Show that a might not reach the base.
Explain: if a is too short (a < b sin A), no triangle exists. If a = b sin A, right triangle. If a ≥ b, one triangle. If between, two triangles.

discoveryHook.scenario: Given two sides and an angle not between them, sometimes no triangle can be formed, sometimes one, and sometimes two different triangles are possible — like a puzzle with multiple solutions.

explanation: SSA means you know two sides and an angle opposite one of them.
Compute height h = b sin A (if A is acute).
If a = h → one right triangle.
If h < a < b → two triangles (ambiguous).
For obtuse A: if a ≤ b, no triangle; if a > b, one triangle.

formulaCard.title: Height formula
notes: h is the perpendicular from C to side c.
If a cannot reach the base, no triangle.

examples.title: A – No triangle
examples.prompt: Show a=15 ft, b=25 ft, A=85° gives no triangle.

examples.title: B – One triangle
examples.prompt: a=22 in, b=12 in, A=42°. Find B.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain: Because a > b, only one triangle exists. Compute sin B and find B acute.

examples.title: C – Two triangles
examples.prompt: a=12 m, b=31 m, A=20.5°. Find both possible B.

confusionCorner.title: Check Supplementary Angle
confusionCorner.body: When using sin⁻¹ to find B, always check if 180° – B also works. If A + (180° – B) < 180°, then two triangles exist.

questions.prompt: In SSA with acute A, compute h = b sin ___. Compare a to h to know how many triangles.
If a = 10, b = 20, A = 30°. What is h? (Enter a number)
hints: Since a = 10 equals h, one right triangle.

questions.prompt: In the ambiguous case, if sin B > 1, the number of triangles is ___.
hints: If sin B is greater than 1, no triangle exists.

blocks.title: Area of an Oblique Triangle
teacherCues: Draw any triangle. Highlight that area = 1/2 × product of two sides × sine of their included angle.
Compare with right triangle area: if the angle is 90°, sin90°=1, giving 1/2 base × height.

discoveryHook.scenario: A triangular garden with two known sides and the angle between them: you can find its area instantly, without measuring a height.

explanation: Works for any triangle, even right triangles (sin90° = 1).

formulaCard.title: Area Formula
notes: Angle must be between the two sides.
If the angle is 90°, area = ½ bc.

examples.title: A – Find area
examples.prompt: Sides 90 m and 52 m, included angle 102°. Find area.

examples.title: B – Choose the formula
examples.prompt: If you know sides a=5, c=8, and angle B=60°, which formula?
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Which two sides are given? Which angle is between them? Write the area expression.
steps: Sides a and c are given; angle B is between them.
Area = ½ × a × c × sin B = ½ × 5 × 8 × sin60° ≈ 17.32.

examples.title: C – Right triangle check
examples.prompt: If C=90°, a=6, b=8, find area using the general formula.
steps: Area = ½ × a × b × sin C = ½ × 6 × 8 × sin90° = ½ × 48 × 1 = 24.

confusionCorner.title: Included Angle Only
confusionCorner.body: Don't use the angle opposite one of the sides. The angle must be the one [[imp:between the two sides]].

questions.prompt: Area = ½ × b × c × sin ___, where A is the angle between b and c.
hints: The angle opposite side a is A.
But here use sides b and c, so include angle A.

questions.prompt: If sides 10 and 14 include an angle of 30°, what is the area? (Enter a number)
hints: The .5 and the ½ multiply to give ¼ of product? Actually ½×10×14 = 70, times 0.5 = 35.

questions.prompt: If the included angle is 90°, the area formula gives the same as ½ × base × height because sin90° = ___.

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid – Boat Race Application
teacherCues: Sketch the course: Start A, B at S 52° W, C at S 40° E, and back to A. C is 8 km south of A.
Use parallel lines to find angles, then Law of Sines.

discoveryHook.scenario: A sailboat race has a triangular course. By knowing one leg and the bearings, you can compute the total distance before leaving the dock.

explanation: [[imp:Understand]]: Draw the triangle. AC = 8 km. From bearings, ∠A = 52°, ∠C = 40°. Then ∠B = 180° – 52° – 40° = 88°.
[[imp:Solve]]: Use Law of Sines with known side b = 8 km opposite B. Find a and c.
[[imp:Conclude]]: Add the three sides to get total distance.

formulaCard.title: Law of Sines (solving for side)
notes: b is known (8 km), B is found (88°).
Plug in A and C to find a and c.

examples.title: A – Understand
examples.prompt: Identify the angles A, B, C from the bearings.
steps: A = bearing angle at A = 52° (south of west).

examples.title: B – Solve
examples.peerPrompt: Work with partner: Use law of sines. Check your calculations with a calculator.

confusionCorner.title: Parallel Lines Help
confusionCorner.body: Because AC is north‑south and BD is parallel, alternate interior angles let you transfer the bearing angles into the triangle.

questions.prompt: In the boat problem, angle B = 180° – 52° – ___°.
What is side a (BC) approximately? (Enter a number like 6.31)
The total race distance is about 19.46 km, which is the sum of a, b, and ___.

challengeCorner.prompt: In the swimming problem: A to B N28°E, B to C N58°W, then back to A directly north. AC = 800 m. Find total distance.
hints: Then use Law of Sines with AC = 800 m.
